claim: The fronto-parietal control network (FPCN) supports cognitive control by coordinating among the demands of the external environment and internal plans.
source: Coordinating among the demands of the external environment and internal plans requires cognitive control supported by a fronto-parietal control network (FPCN).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Multiple control systems span the FPCN whose operations are poorly understood.
source: Evidence suggests that multiple control systems span the FPCN whose operations are poorly understood.
evidence: The abstract cites existing evidence suggesting multiple control systems in the FPCN.

claim: The FPCN consists of an external/present-oriented to internal/future-oriented cortical gradient extending outwardly from sensory-motor cortices.
source: Here, I show that the FPCN consists of an external/present-oriented to internal/future-oriented cortical gradient extending outwardly from sensory-motor cortices.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by activation and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Areas at the ends of the FPCN gradient act in a segregative manner, exciting areas at the same level but suppressing areas at different levels.
source: Areas at the ends of this gradient act in a segregative manner, exciting areas at the same level, but suppressing areas at different levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by effective connectivity analyses showing within-network excitation and between-network suppression at gradient extremes.

claim: Areas in the middle of the FPCN gradient excite areas at all levels, promoting integration of control processing.
source: By contrast, areas in the middle of the gradient excite areas at all levels, promoting integration of control processing.
evidence: This is supported by effective connectivity data showing positive connections from middle areas to all network levels.

claim: Individual differences in integrative dynamics predict higher level cognitive ability.
source: Individual differences in integrative dynamics predict higher level cognitive ability and amenability to neuromodulation.
evidence: This is supported by cross-validated ridge regression analyses showing significant prediction of cognitive ability from integration measures.

claim: Individual differences in integrative dynamics predict amenability to neuromodulation.
source: Individual differences in integrative dynamics predict higher level cognitive ability and amenability to neuromodulation.
evidence: This is supported by analyses showing that integration measures predict TMS susceptibility.

claim: An intermediary zone within the FPCN underlies integrative processing that supports cognitive control.
source: These data suggest that an intermediary zone within the FPCN underlies integrative processing that supports cognitive control.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined findings of activation patterns, effective connectivity, and behavioral predictions.

claim: Cognitive control enables flexible behavior that can adapt to present conditions, prevailing contexts, and future plans.
source: While habits rigidly link stimuli to actions, cognitive control enables flexible behavior that can adapt to present conditions, prevailing contexts, and future plans (Miller and Cohen, 2001; Logan and Gordon, 2001; Egner, 2017; Badre and Nee, 2018).
evidence: This is a foundational concept supported by multiple citations.

claim: The human capacity for flexible behavior arises from the expansion of transmodal cortices that are synaptically distant from primary cortices.
source: The human capacity for flexible behavior is thought to arise from the expansion of transmodal cortices that are synaptically distant from primary cortices (Mesulam, 1998; Margulies et al., 2016; Huntenburg et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Synaptic distance may untether transmodal areas from the processing hierarchies that link stimulus to action in canonical circuits.
source: such that synaptic distance may untether transmodal areas from the processing hierarchies that link stimulus to action in canonical circuits (Buckner and Krienen, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition supported by citation.

claim: Transmodal areas are prominent in the prefrontal (PFC) and posterior parietal cortices (PPC).
source: Such transmodal areas are prominent in the prefrontal (PFC) and posterior parietal cortices (PPC).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about cortical organization.

claim: A co-active set of PFC-PPC areas is frequently termed the 'frontoparietal control network' (FPCN).
source: The relationship between cognitive control and areas of the PFC and PPC is so ubiquitous that a co-active set of PFC-PPC areas is frequently termed the 'frontoparietal control network' (FPCN) (Vincent et al., 2008; Braga and Buckner, 2017; Yeo et al., 2011; Dixon et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a widely accepted terminology supported by multiple citations.

claim: A similar constellation of areas is also referred to as the 'multiple demand network'.
source: Recognizing their involvement across a diverse array of tasks, a similar constellation of areas is also referred to as the 'multiple demand network' (Duncan and Owen, 2000; Duncan, 2010; Duncan, 2013).
evidence: This is an alternative terminology supported by citations.

claim: The FPCN implements cognitive control by flexibly coordinating activity among diverse brain systems to integrate brain-wide processing in a goal-directed manner.
source: This network is thought to implement cognitive control by flexibly coordinating activity among diverse brain systems to integrate brain-wide processing in a goal-directed manner (Murphy et al., 2020; Cole et al., 2013; Cocchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: The integrative capacity of FPCN areas enables them to reconfigure the brain into difficult-to-reach states.
source: The integrative capacity of these areas enables them to reconfigure the brain into difficult-to-reach states (Gu et al., 2015), thereby conferring the flexibility needed to act in an adaptive, rather than habitual manner.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is not a single FPCN, but multiple networks.
source: Mounting evidence suggests that there is not a single FPCN, but multiple networks (Braga and Buckner, 2017; Yeo et al., 2011; Dixon et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: FPCN networks are situated upon global brain gradients such that increasingly sensory-motor distal areas of the PFC and PPC are increasingly distant from areas of the brain involved in external processing.
source: These networks are situated upon global brain gradients such that increasingly sensory-motor distal areas of the PFC and PPC are increasingly distant from areas of the brain involved in external processing (Margulies et al., 2016; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior gradient mapping studies.

claim: The more sensory-motor distal aspects of the FPCN are involved in more internally oriented control processes.
source: This has led to the proposal that the more sensory-motor distal aspects of the FPCN are involved in more internally oriented control processes (Dixon et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a proposal from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Gradients in the PFC and PPC can be classed along an external-internal axis.
source: The proposal that gradients in the PFC and PPC can be classed along an external-internal axis (Sormaz et al., 2018; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019) offers a unifying perspective of the different forms of cognitive control which has remained elusive (Badre and Nee, 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Internally oriented aspects of control must be integrated with externally oriented aspects of control for cognitive control to be grounded in behavior.
source: Ultimately, cognitive control is grounded in behavior. This means that internally oriented aspects of control, such as those that plan for the future, must be integrated with externally oriented aspects of control, such as those that select appropriate sensory features for processing and action.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for behavioral control.

claim: One possibility is that the most sensory-motor distal areas are the most integrative.
source: One possibility is that the control gradient that expands outwardly from sensory-motor cortices doubles as an integration gradient such that the most sensory-motor distal areas are the most integrative.
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical possibility to be tested.

claim: The rostral-most areas act as apex controllers that exert widespread influences that can coordinate brain-wide activity under a single goal.
source: This possibility is consistent with theories of PFC function that posit that the rostral-most (i.e. most sensory-motor distal) areas act as apex controllers that exert widespread influences that can coordinate brain-wide activity under a single goal (Badre and D'Esposito, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical position from prior work supported by citation.

claim: A cascade of control signals progresses from sensory-motor distal to sensory-motor proximal areas with integration of those signals progressing along the way.
source: Another possibility is that a cascade of control signals progresses from sensory-motor distal to sensory-motor proximal areas with integration of those signals progressing along the way (Koechlin et al., 2003; Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007).
evidence: This is an alternative theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Areas situated between externally oriented and internally oriented control are responsible for their integration.
source: A third possibility is that those areas situated between externally oriented and internally oriented control are responsible for their integration.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested and supported by the current study.

claim: Mid-lateral PFC is important for integrative control.
source: This last possibility is consistent with recent data indicating the importance of mid-lateral PFC in integrative control (Badre and Nee, 2018; Cocchi et al., 2014; Nee and D'Esposito, 2016; Nee and D'Esposito, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own studies.

claim: Intermediary zones of the FPCN are essential for flexibly guiding control itself.
source: This latter possibility would suggest a nested structure to gradients in the brain: just as the FPCN is situated in intermediary zones of the brain to flexibly guide sensation to action, so too are intermediary zones of the FPCN essential for flexibly guiding control itself.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference drawn from the hypothesis and supported by the study's findings.

claim: Two datasets have demonstrated macroscale gradients of cognitive control in the PFC.
source: Here, two datasets that have demonstrated macroscale gradients of cognitive control in the PFC (Nee and D'Esposito, 2016; Nee and D'Esposito, 2017) are examined to investigate dynamics in the broader FPCN.
evidence: This refers to prior publications by the author.

claim: The Comprehensive Control Task manipulates three forms of cognitive control across two stimulus domains.
source: These datasets employ a Comprehensive Control Task that manipulates three forms of cognitive control across two stimulus domains to precisely map the functional underpinnings of areas within the FPCN, providing a foundation from which to interpret network dynamics.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: The same gradients of activation observed in the PFC are mirrored in the PPC.
source: The same gradients of activation observed in the PFC are mirrored in the PPC and tied to specific control functions and behavioral timescales.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by activation data.

claim: Gradients of activation are tied to specific control functions and behavioral timescales.
source: The same gradients of activation observed in the PFC are mirrored in the PPC and tied to specific control functions and behavioral timescales.
evidence: This is supported by brain-behavior correlation analyses.

claim: Static and dynamic measures of integration predict trait-level cognitive ability.
source: Finally, static and dynamic measures of integration are used to predict trait-level cognitive ability, and susceptibility of cognitive control to neuromodulation showing the importance of integration for higher-level cognition and interventions more broadly.
evidence: This is supported by cross-validated regression analyses.

claim: Static and dynamic measures of integration predict susceptibility of cognitive control to neuromodulation.
source: Finally, static and dynamic measures of integration are used to predict trait-level cognitive ability, and susceptibility of cognitive control to neuromodulation showing the importance of integration for higher-level cognition and interventions more broadly.
evidence: This is supported by analyses relating integration to TMS effects.

claim: Two independent samples (n = 24, n = 25) completed a Comprehensive Control Task.
source: Two independent samples (n = 24, n = 25) completed a Comprehensive Control Task that independently manipulated demands on stimulus domain (verbal vs spatial processing), sensory-motor control (associating stimuli to actions), contextual control (context-dependence of appropriate stimulus-response associations), and temporal control (planning for the future).
evidence: This describes the sample sizes and task design.

claim: Sensory-motor control, contextual control, and temporal control can be classed along an external-internal continuum.
source: These processes can be classed along an external-internal continuum such that sensory-motor control acts upon the sensory environment, contextual control informs those actions based upon an internalized rule, and temporal control informs the rule based upon an additional internalized representation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conceptual framework illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Sensory-motor control, contextual control, and temporal control can be classed by timescale.
source: These processes can be classed by timescale such that sensory-motor control specifies an action for the present stimulus, contextual control specifies a prevailing task context, and temporal control sustains a prospective memory for the future.
evidence: This is a conceptual classification of the control processes.

claim: The processes are classed by abstraction with sensory-motor control being the most concrete and temporal control being the most abstract.
source: More generally, the processes are classed by abstraction with sensory-motor control being the most concrete and temporal control being the most abstract.
evidence: This is a conceptual classification of the control processes.

claim: In the lateral PFC, activations progressed in a caudal to rostral fashion as a function of abstraction of cognitive control from sensory-motor control, to contextual control, to temporal control.
source: In the lateral PFC, activations progressed in a caudal to rostral fashion as a function of abstraction of cognitive control from sensory-motor control, to contextual control, to temporal control (Nee and D'Esposito, 2016; Nee and D'Esposito, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by activation data shown in Figure 2A and prior publications.

claim: In the PPC, activations progressed in a rostral to caudo-lateral fashion as a function of abstraction of cognitive control.
source: In the PPC, activations progressed in a rostral to caudo-lateral fashion as a function of abstraction of cognitive control (Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by activation data shown in Figure 2A and a prior publication.

claim: In both the lateral PFC and PPC, increasingly abstract control was associated with activations increasingly distant from sensory-motor cortices of the pre/post-central gyri.
source: That is, in both the lateral PFC and PPC, increasingly abstract control was associated with activations increasingly distant from sensory-motor cortices of the pre/post-central gyri.
evidence: This is a summary of the activation gradient findings.

claim: Different cognitive control demands produced overlapping activations eliciting gradients along the lateral surface.
source: Different cognitive control demands produced overlapping activations eliciting gradients along the lateral surface (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar gradients of activation were observed with reduced volumetric smoothing and with minimal, surface-based smoothing.
source: Although the extent of overlap depends upon preprocessing (e.g. smoothing, volumetric vs surface processing), similar gradients of activation were observed with reduced volumetric smoothing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as with minimal, surface-based smoothing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by supplementary figures showing robustness to preprocessing choices.

claim: The mirrored gradients observed in the lateral PFC and PPC are suggestive of a mirrored functional organization extending outwardly from sensory-motor areas consistent with macroscale gradients of cortical function.
source: The mirrored gradients observed in the lateral PFC and PPC are suggestive of a mirrored functional organization extending outwardly from sensory-motor areas consistent with macroscale gradients of cortical function (Mesulam, 1998; Margulies et al., 2016; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior gradient literature.

claim: The FPCN can be fractionated into sub-networks.
source: Previous work has suggested that the FPCN can be fractionated into sub-networks (Braga and Buckner, 2017; Yeo et al., 2011; Dixon et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FPCN network A acts as an intermediary between the FPCN and internally oriented 'default-mode' network (DMN).
source: In particular, it has been proposed that an FPCN network A acts as an intermediary between the FPCN and internally oriented 'default-mode' network (DMN).
evidence: This is a proposal from prior work.

claim: FPCN network B is hypothesized to act as an intermediary to the externally-oriented dorsal attention network (DAN).
source: On the other hand, FPCN network B is hypothesized to act as an intermediary to the externally-oriented dorsal attention network (DAN) (Dixon et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Precise functional descriptions of FPCN sub-networks remains unclear.
source: However, precise functional descriptions of these sub-networks remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Prior work has fractionated the FPCN based on co-activation patterns rather than processing demands.
source: This is because prior work has fractionated the FPCN based on co-activation patterns rather than processing demands.
evidence: This explains the limitation of prior approaches.

claim: Areas activated by temporal control aligned most closely with FPCN A across both samples.
source: Across both samples, areas activated by temporal control aligned most closely with FPCN A (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through network overlap analysis.

claim: Areas activated by both contextual control and sensory-motor control aligned most closely with FPCN B.
source: By contrast, areas activated by both contextual control and sensory-motor control aligned most closely with FPCN B.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through network overlap analysis.

claim: Areas activated by sensory-motor control activated the DAN more extensively.
source: While areas activated by contextual control also activated FPCN A to some degree, areas activated by sensory-motor control activated the DAN more extensively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through network overlap analysis.

claim: The task contrasts fractionate the FPCN into sub-networks along an external (DAN -> FPCN B) to internal (FPCN A -> DMN) axis.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the task contrasts fractionate the FPCN into sub-networks along an external (DAN -> FPCN B) to internal (FPCN A -> DMN) axis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the network overlap findings.

claim: PFC-PPC areas closer to sensory-motor cortex tended to be sensitive to multiple demands activating for both sensory-motor and contextual control.
source: PFC-PPC areas closer to sensory-motor cortex (blue, green) tended to be sensitive to multiple demands activating for both sensory-motor and contextual control.
evidence: This is shown in the activation profiles in Figure 3A.

claim: PFC-PPC areas closer to sensory-motor cortex had a tendency to activate preferentially to one stimulus domain or the other.
source: These areas also had a tendency to activate preferentially to one stimulus domain or the other.
evidence: This is shown in the activation profiles in Figure 3A.

claim: Areas distal from sensory-motor cortices tended to be more specialized toward temporal control and did not show a preference for stimulus domain.
source: By contrast, areas distal from sensory-motor cortices (red) tended to be more specialized toward temporal control and did not show a preference for stimulus domain.
evidence: This is shown in the activation profiles in Figure 3A.

claim: Two dimensions of multi-dimensional scaling accounted for 89% of the variance of the ROI data.
source: Two dimensions accounted for 89% of the variance of the data (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result of the MDS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The first dimension of MDS recapitulated the abstraction gradient.
source: The first dimension recapitulated the abstraction gradient, placing PFC-PPC areas proximal to sensory-motor cortices on one end of the dimension (e.g. superior frontal sulcus - SFS; anterior intra-parietal sulcus - aIPS), and areas distal to sensory-motor cortices on the other (e.g. middle frontal gyrus - MFG; inferior parietal lobule - IPL).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and described in the text.

claim: The second dimension of MDS reflected sensitivity to stimulus domain.
source: The second dimension reflected sensitivity to stimulus domain with areas preferentially engaged by spatial processing at one end and areas preferentially engaged by verbal processing at the other.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and described in the text.

claim: The cortex is organized along two principle gradients reflecting abstraction and modality.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that the cortex is organized along two principle gradients reflecting abstraction and modality (Mesulam, 1998; Margulies et al., 2016; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the MDS results and citations to prior gradient literature.

claim: In the PFC, increasing rostral areas were increasingly associated with future behavior and decreasingly associated with present behavior.
source: In the PFC, increasing rostral areas were increasingly associated with future behavior and decreasingly associated with present behavior (Nee and D'Esposito, 2016; Nee and D'Esposito, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by brain-behavior correlations and prior publications.

claim: This pattern was mirrored in the PPC such that sensory-motor proximal areas were positively associated with present, but not future behavior, while sensory-motor distal areas were positively associated with future, but not present behavior.
source: This pattern was mirrored in the PPC (Figure 4A) such that sensory-motor proximal areas (aIPS, SPL) were positively associated with present, but not future behavior, while sensory-motor distal areas (IPL) were positively associated with future, but not present behavior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through repeated measures correlations.

claim: Areas in-between sensory-motor proximal and distal areas were associated with both present and future behavior.
source: Areas in-between (mIPS) were associated with both present and future behavior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through repeated measures correlations.

claim: The more abstract the PFC-PPC area, the less it related to current behavior.
source: Consistent with the impressions above, the more abstract the PFC-PPC area, the less it related to current behavior (sample 1: t(238) = −9.18, p=2.19e-17; sample 2: t(248) = −8.73, p=3.81e-16)
evidence: This is supported by linear mixed effects modeling using the MDS abstraction dimension.

claim: The more abstract the PFC-PPC area, the more it related to future behavior.
source: and more it related to future behavior (sample 1: t(238) = 2.72, p=0.007; sample 2: t(248) = 4.39, p=0.00002).
evidence: This is supported by linear mixed effects modeling using the MDS abstraction dimension.

claim: The abstraction-behavior relationships were observed when each stimulus domain was treated separately consistent with domain-generality of these patterns.
source: Moreover, the abstraction-behavior relationships were observed when each stimulus domain was treated separately consistent with domain-generality of these patterns (verbal abstraction-current sample 1: t(238) = −6.61, p=2.52e-10; sample 2: t(248) = −8.11, p=2.38e-14; spatial abstraction-current sample 1: t(238) = −10.21, p=1.55e-20; sample 2: t(248) = −7.87, p=1.07e-13; verbal abstraction-future sample 1: t(238) = 3.05, p=0.003; sample 2: t(248) = 3.77, p=0.0002; spatial abstraction-future sample 1: t(238) = 2.29, p=0.01; sample 2: t(248) = 4.23, p=3.32e-5).
evidence: This is supported by additional linear mixed effects models.

claim: Progressively abstract areas in both the PFC and PPC are increasingly future-oriented.
source: Hence, these analyses indicate that progressively abstract areas in both the PFC and PPC are increasingly future-oriented.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the brain-behavior analyses.

claim: Estimates of directed interactions had excellent correspondence across the samples (r = 0.96).
source: These estimates had excellent correspondence across the samples (r = 0.96; Figure 5, top).
evidence: This validates the effective connectivity method by showing replicability.

claim: The magnitude of effective connectivity arising from the PFC was significantly stronger than that arising from the PPC.
source: In both samples, the magnitude of effective connectivity arising from the PFC was significantly stronger than that arising from the PPC (sample 1: F(1,23) = 7.1, p=0.0138; sample 2: F(1,24) = 6.26, p=0.0195; Figure 5, bottom).
evidence: This is shown through analysis of effective connectivity by source-target lobe pairs.

claim: The PFC is the primary driver of PFC-PPC dynamics.
source: Such data are consistent with the idea that the PFC is the primary driver of PFC-PPC dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the effective connectivity findings.

claim: A significant source x target network interaction was observed in effective connectivity in both samples.
source: In both samples, a significant source x target network interaction was observed in effective connectivity (sample 1: F(4,46) = 25.1, p=4.56e-14; sample 2: F(4,48) = 17.81, p=5.74e-11; Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown through ANOVA of effective connectivity by network.

claim: Within-network directed interactions were significant and numerically the most positive connections for each network.
source: In all cases, within-network directed interactions were significant and numerically the most positive connections for each network.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and validates the network assignments.

claim: For both nodes in the abstract, temporal control network and the concrete, sensory-motor control network, between-network directed interactions tended to be negative.
source: For both nodes in the abstract, temporal control network and the concrete, sensory-motor control network, between-network directed interactions tended to be negative.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 through network-level effective connectivity analysis.

claim: Temporal control and sensory-motor control networks dampen activity in other networks, thereby segregating processing.
source: Such patterns suggest that these networks dampen activity in other networks, thereby segregating processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative between-network connections.

claim: Between-network directed interactions arising from contextual control nodes were significantly positive.
source: By contrast, between-network directed interactions arising from contextual control nodes were significantly positive (Figure 6 – top panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 through network-level effective connectivity analysis.

claim: The contextual control network elevates activity in other networks, thereby promoting integrative processing.
source: Such patterns suggest that the contextual control network elevates activity in other networks, thereby promoting integrative processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the positive between-network connections from contextual control.

claim: The integration dynamics were not driven by task-related signals.
source: Control analyses revealed that these dynamics were not driven by task-related signals since regressing out task-related activity demonstrated the same pattern of results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through control analyses in supplementary figures.

claim: A significant source x target abstraction interaction was observed in both samples.
source: In both samples, a significant source x target abstraction interaction was observed (sample 1: t(1097) = 5.08, p=4.43e-07; sample 2: t(1143) = 4.94, p=9.03e-07)
evidence: This is shown through linear mixed effects modeling using the MDS abstraction dimension.

claim: There was a quadratic effect of source abstraction in both samples.
source: Critically, there was also a quadratic effect of source abstraction (sample 1: t(1097) = −4.51, p=7.05e-06; sample 2: t(1143) = −4.52, p=6.99e-06)
evidence: This is shown through linear mixed effects modeling.

claim: Areas at mid-levels of abstraction have consistently positive outwards influences, while areas at high and low levels of abstraction demonstrate both positive and negative outward influences.
source: which was driven by areas at mid-levels of abstraction having consistently positive outwards influences, while areas at high and low levels of abstraction demonstrated both positive and negative outward influences which yielded lower net influences when averaged (Figure 6 – bottom panel).
evidence: This explains the quadratic effect and is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Context-independent effective connectivity estimates were replicable (r = 0.86).
source: Validation of the method by comparing estimates across samples (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) indicated that the context-independent effective connectivity estimates were replicable (r = 0.86)
evidence: This validates the PPI method by showing replicability.

claim: PPI's of temporal control showed modest replicability (r = 0.32).
source: PPI's of temporal control showed modest replicability (r = 0.32)
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: PPI's of contextual control showed strong replicability (r = 0.78).
source: and PPI's of contextual control showed strong replicability (r = 0.78).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: PPI's of sensory-motor control were not replicable (r = −0.06).
source: PPI's of sensory-motor control were not replicable (r = −0.06).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Areas engaged by sensory-motor control could largely be recapitulated by contrasts of stimulus domain.
source: However, those areas engaged by sensory-motor control could largely be recapitulated by contrasts of stimulus domain (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: PPI's of stimulus domain showed strong replicability (r = 0.88).
source: PPI's of stimulus domain showed strong replicability (r = 0.88).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Within-network PPI's were generally weak across demands.
source: In contrast to the stationary dynamics, within-network PPI's were generally weak across demands (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Within-network interactions are weakly modulated by task demands.
source: This indicates that within-network interactions are weakly modulated by task demands, which has been previously been observed in functional connectivity (Cole et al., 2014; Krienen et al., 2014; Gratton et al., 2016).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Stronger modulations were observed between networks which was especially prominent during contextual control.
source: Stronger modulations were observed between networks which was especially prominent during contextual control.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: There was a main effect of network connectivity driven by stronger between- than within-network connectivity.
source: This analysis revealed a main effect of network connectivity (sample 1: F(1,23) = 15.01, p=0.0008; sample 2: F(1,24) = 10.34, p=0.0037), driven by stronger between- than within-network connectivity.
evidence: This is shown through ANOVA of PPI data.

claim: There was a network connectivity x contrast interaction.
source: However, there was a network connectivity x contrast interaction (sample 1: F(2,46) = 11.84, p=0.0001; sample 2: F(2,48) = 9.86, p=0.0003).
evidence: This is shown through ANOVA of PPI data.

claim: The network connectivity x contrast interaction was driven by stronger between-network connectivity for the contextual control contrast relative to the other contrasts.
source: This interaction was driven by stronger between-network connectivity for the contextual control contrast relative to the other contrasts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Contextual control is associated with integration across PFC-PPC networks.
source: These results demonstrate that contextual control is associated with integration across PFC-PPC networks (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PPI analyses shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A significant prediction effect was observed (r = 0.32, p=0.029) indicating that individual differences in integration dynamics are related to higher level cognitive ability.
source: A significant prediction effect was observed (r = 0.32, p=0.029; Figure 8D) indicating that individual differences in integration dynamics are related to higher level cognitive ability.
evidence: This is shown through cross-validated ridge regression.

claim: Static integration was associated with lower cognitive ability.
source: While static integration was associated with lower cognitive ability, dynamic integration was associated with higher cognitive ability (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8E through correlations.

claim: Dynamic integration was associated with higher cognitive ability.
source: While static integration was associated with lower cognitive ability, dynamic integration was associated with higher cognitive ability (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8E through correlations.

claim: Activation-based measures were able to predict individual differences in higher-level cognitive ability (r = 0.37, p=0.01).
source: Similar to the integration measures, activation measures were able to predict individual differences in higher-level cognitive ability (r = 0.37, p=0.01; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Activation-based measures were complementary to network integration measures.
source: However, activation-based measures were complementary to network integration measures as evidenced by insignificant shared variance amongst the measures (activations explained ~3% of variance in the integration measures, adjusted R-square <0).
evidence: This is shown through variance partitioning analyses.

claim: Adding activation measures to the network integration measures significantly improved prediction accuracy (r = 0.50, p=0.002).
source: Moreover, adding activation measures to the network integration measures significantly improved prediction accuracy (r = 0.50, p=0.002; nested model comparison using ordinary regression: F(4,42) = 2.84, p=0.048).
evidence: This is shown through nested model comparison.

claim: With reduced smoothing, no relationship was observed among cognitive ability and static integration.
source: Although dynamic integration was again positively associated with cognitive ability, with reduced smoothing, no relationship was observed among cognitive ability and static integration. As a result, integration measures could not be used to predict cognitive ability (r = 0.03; p=0.44; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures with reduced smoothing.

claim: TMS effects on cognitive control could be predicted by static and dynamic integration (r = 0.56, p=0.01).
source: This analysis revealed that TMS effects on cognitive control could be predicted by static and dynamic integration (r = 0.56, p=0.01; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown through leave-one-out cross-validated ridge regression.

claim: Individuals with stronger static integration tended to show increased TMS-induced cognitive control impairments.
source: In particular, those individuals with stronger static integration tended to show increased TMS-induced cognitive control impairments, while those individuals with stronger dynamic integration tended to show decreased TMS-induced cognitive control impairments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B through correlations.

claim: Individuals with stronger dynamic integration tended to show decreased TMS-induced cognitive control impairments.
source: In particular, those individuals with stronger static integration tended to show increased TMS-induced cognitive control impairments, while those individuals with stronger dynamic integration tended to show decreased TMS-induced cognitive control impairments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B through correlations.

claim: Integration of control networks is related to susceptibility to neuromodulation.
source: Such data indicate that integration of control networks is related to susceptibility to neuromodulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the TMS prediction analyses.

claim: Integration measures predicted TMS susceptibility over-and-above cognitive ability.
source: To examine whether integration measures predicted TMS susceptibility over-and-above cognitive ability, cognitive ability was regressed out of measures of static and dynamic integration. The resultant measures could be used to predict TMS susceptibility (r = 0.46, p=0.02; Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown through control analyses in supplementary figures.

claim: Activation-based measures could not predict TMS susceptibility.
source: Unlike cognitive ability, activation-based measures could not predict TMS susceptibility (correlations among predicted and observed TMS effects all <0; Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Network integration is useful for predicting susceptibility to neuromodulation over-and-above cognitive ability and control-related activations.
source: Hence, these data suggest that network integration is useful for predicting susceptibility to neuromodulation over-and-above cognitive ability and control-related activations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the TMS prediction analyses.
